utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances for the day, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, assisted by Crispian Smith, Case Manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Ivana Batista.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, can I just mention very shortly two, maybe three, matters. The first is this. We hadn't forgotten that last week Judge Delvoie asked us for a list of witnesses up to the adjournment. That will be with the Court and the Defence hopefully in fact tomorrow. We're just refining the last few witnesses. The second matter is this, and I think I've mentioned on one or two occasions before, we will be filing a motion next week in respect of the witnesses we wish to add to replace the adjudicated facts which were not granted or reversed. Your Honours, of necessity we have to explain why we say the witnesses are necessary, refer to the adjudicated facts and to the matters on the indictment, and we would ask for an extension of the word limit in this case. Could we have an extension up to 5.000 words. I don't think we'll need 5.000, but just to be safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the last matter is this, I don't want to delay today's witness, because of the videolink, but I would like to invite Your Honours to reconsider yesterday's ruling when he's finished. I don't anticipate that he is going to take as long as the Defence said from conversations, certainly, that I've had with Mr. Krgovic. And I've had an opportunity now to read the cases that were referred to -- to by Mr. O'Sullivan, and I would like, if I may, to ask Your Honours, as I say, to reconsider the ruling in respect of yesterday. But, as I say, that can wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's about -- sorry. I didn't make it clear obviously. The ruling Your Honours made about the non-admittance of any of the articles yesterday. However, I forgot to mention that, Your Honours, we've had no ruling on document which is tab 52, at the moment, on the list for today's witness. Can I say straight away, although we did file this some time ago and I have reminded the legal officer about this, and indeed reminded him against yesterday, I don't need to use it with this witness but it will be used by the witness who is coming next week. Subject to Your Honours' ruling, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 52 of today's witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours will see, it says there -- it formed part of a motion which I'm not going to go into because we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is it 65 ter number 2839?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see the Court Officer on the screen, and I need her, first of all, to confirm that she can hear us in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, the connection is working ... and I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I take it that the witness is there with you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The witness is not here in the witness room because I was informed that there were procedural matters. I will bring him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, the witness is present in the courtroom -- in the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would now invite the Court Officer to have you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare I will only speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, you may resume your seat. The declaration that you would have just made binds you as a witness to testify truthfully under pain of -- of -- of the power that the Tribunal has to deal with false testimony. I would begin by asking to you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Branko Peric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your date of birth is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] January 10, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a lawyer by profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You, as -- as may have been explained to you, as would have been explained to you, you are, although not physically present in The Hague, are now sworn as a witness in the proceedings of the Tribunal and the Tribunal is receiving your evidence by videolink. The -- you would have given evidence previously before the Tribunal and/or in one of the countries in the region. Would you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's a judge --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's a judge at the State Court. He is not a -- he's never given evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Oh. Thank you, Ms. Korner. The -- I would explain the procedure to you. The -- and you would be aware of this, having regard to your own profession, that the side calling - in this case, the Prosecution - would begin by asking you questions. And, in terms were time, the amount of time that has been allotted to them is two and a half hours in total. After which the counsel for each of the accused would have an opportunity to cross-examine you, and they have asked for a total of five hours between themselves. After which there may be re-examination and the Chamber may have some questions of you. In order to expedite the record-keeping and the other ancillary matters that support the way witnesses -- testimonies are led at the Tribunal, the sittings do not ordinarily extend beyond an hour and a half and indeed are a few minutes short of that. And so we would take a break initially at the -- after about an hour and 20 minutes then, in 20 minutes we would resume, and then there is another session of similar length, and we would adjourn for the day at 7.00 the -- local time, by local time I mean the time in The Hague, and you are scheduled to continue your testimony tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the -- again I'm using local time. Now not withstanding what I would have just said in terms of regular and usual times of sittings and breaks, if, at any time, there is a need for you to take a break for whatever reason, if you would indicate to the Court Officer who is with you, and the Chamber will deal with -- will seek to accommodate you. Do you have any questions before I invite counsel for the Prosecution to begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge Peric, good afternoon. Can we start, please, by --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we start, please, by having up on the screen, please, the biography that you kindly provided us, which is 10359.03, and it's at tab 77 bis of the document binder. Tab 77 bis for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so if we see your professional history, as you told the Court, you were a lawyer. Then for our purposes the relevant time is that you were a -- the public prosecutor in Teslic between May of 1992 and June of 1995. I think that made --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then do you become a journalist and then return to the law as a, first of all, a member of the High Judicial and Prosecutorial Council in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You then became a judge in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Court in 2003. You are still there. And you were also for four years president of the Bosnian High Judicial and Prosecutorial Council; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think that council has the responsibility of selecting the judges and prosecutors who are authorised to appear in the State Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, again briefly, can I deal -- sorry, before I do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether you think this something that's worth having exhibited. I've given the material parts of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does it add to anything that's on the record? I suppose for the sake of convenience it doesn't hurt to have it but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, may it -- can it be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, as a matter of form, Judge Peric, I have to ask you about your interviews. I think it's right that you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, first of all, in December of 2001. Then again in January of 2002, and finally made a short witness statement in February of last year. In respect of those interviews a statement --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In respect of those interviews and the statement if you were asked the same questions again, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was what you told the Prosecutor then the truth?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want briefly with you to run through the aspects of the evidence you gave in those interviews because I do not, except with a few exceptions, want to go through them with you again. You will, no doubt, be happy to hear. You dealt with the relationship between the Teslic Crisis Staff, the Assembly, and the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You dealt with what you knew of Radoslav Brdjanin and the SDS leadership, with work obligation, the operation of the judicial system, the relationship between military and civilian courts, the destruction of religious buildings, the role of the police. You had quite a lot to say about the decision of the Municipal Assembly in Teslic that was passed -- the meeting of the 6th of July, 1992. You dealt with disarmament and the charges of armed rebellion. You dealt with dismissal of non-Serbs, the departure of non-Serbs from Teslic, the attacks on Stenjak and Rankovici, and in detail, and I will cover some of that with you, the Mice. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, may I ask that the 92 ter package, the proper one as -- as displayed on our last exhibit list may be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought that Mr. Pantelic was rising to make an objection. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P1361.01 to P1361.12, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Judge, can we -- I'm going to ask you to look at some further documents that you had an opportunity to look at some time ago. But first can we clarify this. The Court has heard that on the 6th of April 1992, the Teslic Assembly applied to become a part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. In fact said it did. Did the prosecutor's office in Teslic then come under the Banja Luka authority or that -- or did it remain with Doboj?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor's office remained with Doboj and functioned as basic prosecutor office in Teslic under the jurisdiction of the higher office in Doboj. The same applied to the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can I ask you then next, please, to have a look at a document, which is tab 7 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's 0085 -- 65 ter 850.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a decision of the Executive Committee of the Teslic municipality, which imposes a curfew, starting on the 5th of May, 1992, and it's imposed between 2300 and 0500 hours. Do you recall a curfew being enforced?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think it was. Although there was another situation when curfew was imposed, but I think that was in the period of Mices.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The curfew, who enforced it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: The decision was as I can see reached by the Executive Committee but I think it was enforced by the police. The police and I think it was the department for National Defence at the time was in charge of handing out passes for those people who were under work obligation or who had some specific assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to come onto your work obligation in a moment, but if -- were people -- was anybody, sorry, "were people." Was anyone given any kind of pass that would enable them to ignore the curfew?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that some people did have passes, but I couldn't say exactly who.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then I won't press --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: In this period --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I keep forgetting about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours could this document which I don't believe has been exhibited yet be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, next, can we go, please, to document which has already been exhibited as P1353.06. Oh, tab 8. I'm so sorry. Tab 8. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a record of a Crisis Staff meeting that took place on the 6th of May, 1992. Now, you said in interview Mr. -- Judge Peric, that you had attended one Crisis Staff meeting, you thought in May, and it had taken place in the basement of the municipal building. Are you able to say whether this was the one you attended? It deals with, among other things, work obligation, and, we'll see, a couple of other things.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No. It can't have been this meeting, because I believe it was on the 25th of May that I assumed my position, and this was on the 6th of May. Now, the meeting that you mean may have taken place toward the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In -- can I ask you about one -- two aspects. The first is that 1.6 of this meeting under the agenda, is -- it's 1.6 which is on the first page, says: "Introduce work obligation in all businesses and institutions ..." "And then all citizens are liable for work obligation if so decided by the TO Staff Command." Now as far as that work obligation was concerned, was this a voluntary thing, or was it something that was effectively ordered?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think it was an obligation. Documents were issued by the TO Staff, so this was not a voluntary obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, by and large, who was made to do work obligation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Mostly people who worked in manufacturing processes or who worked for some institutions. There must have been some criteria that were applied, but I cannot speak about the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were -- was this work obligation, what sort of work did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the people had to do the work that they used to do in companies or government bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Or -- or they may have been assigned to do some other work. It is possible that they were assigned to some other jobs that they used not to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody was assigned to do jobs such as digging trenches or the like, which might take them into the front line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which period, if I may ask? To what time-period are you referring in your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Between April 1992 and the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: More certainly there was this type of work obligation in that period. I was even able to see people in some collection centres, and I heard that they were to go off for some work obligation. This work also involved going to the line but where and how, I don't know. However, this is only what I heard, so this is not first-hand information. I saw at some locations that there were people -- people had been taken there and waiting for some sort of schedule.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you say you saw some people in some collection centres. What sort of people? In other words, what nationality were those people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Those were citizens of Croat and Muslim ethnic affiliations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know -- could you name the collection centres that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: One location was in the centre of town. It's the handball pitch of the Proletar Club, and another was at Banja Lisica about 3 kilometres from Teslic where there are tennis grounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, could you turn to 1.8 of this meeting. And I think that's still on the same page. Yes, it is. It's at the bottom of the page in B/C/S. "All paramilitary formations and individuals illegally possessing arms and ammunition are called upon to hand them over to the municipal TO Staff or the nearest military unit immediately or by no later than 1500 hours on the 11th of May ..." "After the expiry of this deadline, responsible organs will search and confiscate arms and ammunition, applying the most rigorous sanctions." Now, you spoke about the disarmament process during the course of -- of your interview at the -- the second interview this is, at page 54. But I'd just like to ask you a few more questions about that. First, against whom was the call for disarmament applied? Which sections of the population?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the sort of arms that were being taken from them, did you, on occasion, see what sort of weapons they were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No, I had no opportunity to see them. I only heard stories on the occasion of the military police operation at the Rankovici village that weapons were brought in on tractors. But I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, as a prosecutor in Teslic, non-Serbs who were found with arms, for what offence were they prosecuted? Or what charges were brought against them.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that this criminal offence was called illegal possession of weapons and explosive substances. I don't remember the exact article in the Criminal Code. But this would have been the criminal offence in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to come onto some -- to your books and the Code -- the offences in a moment. But as far as you were concerned, what sort of evidence did the police provide you with, in respect of these people who were arrested for illegal possession of -- of arms?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that those were certificates about the seizure of weapons. That was the only evidence that was enclosed with the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you yourself aware of how some of the non-Serbs had acquired arms, which were not, say, for example, hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I can only suppose that there was substantial quantity of hunting weapons for which they had valid permits and that the police would seize those even from persons who had permits. I heard, however, that some military armaments were taken away from Croats and Muslims in that period and that there was a flourishing trade in these armaments; namely, that Serbs sold them to Muslims and Croats and that they came by their weapons in this manner, that is, through illicit trade. But this is only a story that I was able to hear. I have no other source of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where such -- as far as you understood it, and I accept that you didn't have first-hand information, where such a sale will taken place, would the police be aware of who had sold what weapons to whom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak about that. I allow for the possibility ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Don't worry. Thank you very much, judge. We'll move to a separate document. Thank you. Now, I want to ask you, please, a few questions about the judicial system itself at this period of time. That is, 1992. Again, you dealt with it in your interview, but I think it may help the Court if we just cover a few of the salient points.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in 1992, was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is at page 16 of the first interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- was it the police who decided who would be prosecuted? In other words, they were the first port of call for an investigation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. One could say that they were the first link in the chain. But because under the law they were in charge of collecting evidence about criminal offences. And it was the public prosecutor who launched the continuation of the process. So the prosecutor could be seen as something of a go-between, between the police and the court, although the prosecutor did have some powers to launch some investigations. However, in practice, most times public prosecutors limited themselves to processing the criminal reports received from the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So once the police had investigated, would they then submit a criminal report to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were even authorised to impose detention for up to three days. It was so-called police detention before filing a criminal report with the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And was it then the prosecutor's decision whether, based on the documents or the evidence produced, that there was sufficient evidence to -- for the police to charge the person with a -- a crime.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The prosecutor would consider the evidence enclosed with the criminal report and then decide whether to refuse it or launch an investigation. In case of less serious offences, there was the possibility of skipping the investigation stage and going directly to an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can I come now to the -- the question of this known and unknown perpetrator. If the police sent up a file that said, "perpetrator unknown," what further steps could the prosecutor take?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, there weren't many options. Mostly it boiled down to an order to the police to continue collecting evidence and engage in activities necessary to identify the perpetrator. Such cases were filed as criminal reports against unknown perpetrators, and we would wait for information to come in about the perpetrator. That information would come from the police, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, from your own experiences in Teslic in 1992 - and I'm limiting the question to 1992 - what view did you form about the number of unknown perpetrator cases that came to you as the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that a smaller number of those was filed. Most perpetrators were not reported. Here, I rely on a report that I made in that period, in which I stated that many perpetrators remained unidentified. It was my suspicion that the police did not report all perpetrators of crimes who were known, and that is why I demanded from the police and other institutions that all cases be processed. I based this upon what I was able to hear in the -- in that period. There was a large number of criminal offences for which it could be supposed that the police did know the perpetrator was never reported. Such as planting explosive devices, breaking and entering, theft of automobiles, and other criminal offences. I believe I stated all that in my report --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: -- and it was my position that this situation cannot be tolerated. I insisted that the police do their work the way they are expected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we're going to have a look at your report a little later because it came in September of 1992. So if the police gave you a file which had an unknown perpetrator, there was nothing further that you, the prosecutor, could do other than presumably tell the police to carry on investigating?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor had absolutely no way of doing anything independently from the police, and that was the problem with that system. The police could simply say, Based on available information, we're unable to identify the perpetrator. And the prosecutor had no resources of his own to conduct an independent investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've said that was the problem with the system then. Has the -- just so that we can see the contrast. Has the system changed since then? Since 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: The system changed after 2000 when the -- when the criminal legislation was reformed. Under the new system the public prosecutor runs the investigation; he has just authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you. All right. That's all for the moment I want to ask you about the general picture of the judicial system. We're going to look at some files and your log-books a little later. Can I ask you now, please, to deal, however, with the jurisdictional overlap, as it were, between -- sorry, between cases that came within the civilian courts and those that came within the military courts?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up on the screen - and it's your tab 1, please - the Law on Military Courts, which is P1284.07. And could we go in that, please, to Article, please, 15 which is on the third -- third page in English, and, in B/C/S, it is the third page as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Article 15 deals with the respective jurisdictions of the military court and civilian court. And there we see, it says that: "If a serviceman and a civilian exclusive of persons under Article 13," which deals with the various crimes that are excluded, and we've been through those with another witness, "had committed a crime as accomplices, and if the trial of the civilian falls within the jurisdiction of another regular court, this court will also try the serviceman. In your experience and your knowledge, where there was a mixed group - for example, the Mice, which were mixed members of the civilian police and the military, would the civilian court have jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that in the relevant period, we had authority. That is, the regular jurisdiction -- or, rather, judiciary. Because the military court did not function. I cannot remember now when it was established and started functioning. For a while, I believe they existed but they didn't have any judges except for the president. I think his name was Mile Vignjevic as far as I remember. But I cannot say when it started discharging its authority. In case of the Mice, if we were to adhere to the law strictly, the military court would have jurisdiction. But that question never arose because -- probably because the military court was not functioning yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But as far as Article 15 is concerned, could -- from your experience, could the civilian courts also try where there was a crime that had been committed by both civilians and members of the military, could the civilian courts try both? That is to say, the civilian and the military person.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I believe so. The question of jurisdiction could arise in the course of the proceedings, but here it did not arise. There were a large number of civilian persons, that is, from the police, and the conclusion was that this falls under the jurisdiction of the regular judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, as far as the question of war crimes is concerned, and that's Article 13, which is on -- begins on the second page of the English version of this, and I believe also in the B/C/S. Yep. Did the civilian courts have jurisdiction over war crimes which were committed by civilians obviously with the exception of prisoners of war, which is excluded specifically?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I believe that military courts had the jurisdiction over war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But is that all war crimes; or did the civilian courts have jurisdiction over war crimes when they were committed, as we see in Article 13, by civilians who didn't come within any of the -- as you call it -- I suppose -- yes, subsections of that Article?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the witness is being shown something that may lead him to a wrong conclusion. In Article 13, war crimes are not mentioned. So the witness should first be asked which crime -- criminal offences are dealt with in Article 13 and only then ask him about war crimes specifically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer your question completely with full responsibility. I wouldn't know which offences were encompassed by Article 13, and I also don't know whether the war crimes fall exclusively under the jurisdiction of military courts. And based on these basic provisions, I cannot conclude what the answer should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Judge, I thought you had taken through this when you were seen. But if you haven't, rather than go through because the time is limited that I have with you, all of the various sections that are enumerated, we'll leave that. Are you aware of any prosecutions against civilians who were Serbs for any war crimes committed against the non-Serb population in Teslic, other than the Mice Group, which we'll come onto.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know of such cases, and I don't think there were any.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That deals with that aspect. Now, can I move, please, to look at the Mice saga. You dealt with this again in your interview at some length, and it's the second interview from page 33 onwards. But I want you to have a look at some of the documents that you weren't shown at the time of the interview. Can I just ask you this. We -- we know that the Mice Group was arrested by Predrag Radulovic who came from Banja Luka together with a group of men in order to affect that arrest. Do you have any recollection now of whether or not you attended a meeting in Banja Luka with Mr. Perisic, president of the municipality, and others, about dealing with the Mice?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember attending such a meeting, together with the president of the court, the president of the municipality, Mr. Perisic, and I think Mr. Radulovic was also present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I just ask you this, because it's a question that's come up before, do you know where the name "Mice" came from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I have heard stories, allegedly, that was the diminutive version of Milan Ninkovic's name who was the leader in Doboj, and so Milan, nickname Mica, and then hence Mices. That's what I heard but I cannot claim it as truth. It does sound logical though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let move straight, shall we, then, please, to the file -- well, actually let's start with the -- oh, no documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at -- well, first of all, at document 10361. Your Honours, it's not obviously on our 65 ter list and I'm not going ask for it to be exhibited at this stage. Sorry, tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a report dated the 5th of June from someone called Milos. You'll see it on the back of it. And I just want to ask you about this. It says in this report: "About 50 Muslims and Croats have been arrested in Teslic. There is information that they were responsible for the organisation and creation of enemy military formations and the organisers of weapons procurement and distribution." From your own knowledge of what happened in Teslic, does that refer to arrests by members of the Mice Group or to some other arrests?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No, I think this must be about some other persons, not about members of Mice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So -- no. Yeah, this 5th of June, do you know whether, were the police or other authority --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this may refer to the action in the village of Stenjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, I'll come back to it, because, as I say, I want to deal with Stenjak separately. All right. Next, can we move, please, then, to the next document which is at your tab 11, and it's P702. It is already exhibited. Now, this is a military report of the 1st of July, but I want to ask you about a couple of things in it, if you can assist us. At page 3 in English, and, in B/C/S, it is the second page, there's a paragraph that says: "A special unit for combatting DTG," which appears to be sabotage groups, "and securing vital buildings of some 60 men was formed as part of a CJB in February 1992. As a large number of the delinquents became a part of the unit immediately after its formation, there were reactions from the locals in Teslic regarding the inappropriate behaviour of its members." Now, do you know anything about that, about this special unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think there were people who were in charge of securing communications, bridges, and some facilities. I assume this refers to the people like that who also conducted searches at check-points on communications route -- communications. I know for a fact there were check-points on roads --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: -- held or manned by armed people, and I assume that this refers to the people like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And it says: "A large number of delinquents and so there were reactions from locals in Teslic." Do you recall that people reacted badly to delinquents being part of this group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No, no, I really don't have any recollection on that. But I would allow for the possibility that there were a large number of people there who did have a criminal record of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And final question on this then is, do you know under whose authority this special unit came, who were securing communications, bridges, and the like?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't think that they arrived Teslic. I think they were established in Teslic, but I don't know who they were established by, in what way, at what time, how many men did they have among their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then it goes on to deal with the Mice, the military aspect of the Mice, in the paragraph after that that Captain First-Class Ljubisa Petricevic, former head of the Doboj military section, was sent from Doboj to Teslic at the end of May 1992 ... brought military police with him. And Petricevic and this group carried out a successful mobilisation in several days. Was mobilisation part of what this group were doing, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, I didn't have information to that effect, namely that they've come there for the purpose of mobilisation. What was obvious was the other part, the other side of the coin, the criminal element. I do not know of any mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all I ask about that document. And now can we look, please, at the whole of the Mice file. You will find it at your tab 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through the whole of it, but we'll just go through some of it. Oh, sorry, it's Exhibit 65 ter 2485.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've had a chance to look through this, Judge Peric, before. Can you confirm that this is the file on the Mice Group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, may I ask that this now be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it contains a number of documents, the majority of which, I think, are statements taken from the persons, some of the persons who were arrested, and also statements from potential witnesses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And some of them - is this right? - are -- some of the statements, not all of them are there, but some of the statements taken were from victims of this Group's crimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And others who were in a position to know them. Now, I want to look, please, just at the statement of one of the people who was actually arrested, and that's Mr. Tekic. You will find that in, I think, page 17 of the file. I hope. Oh, it's all going one towards -- but quite difficult. It's 17 pages in and it's page 24 in the English and 17 of B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I'll give you the ERN number at the top, that's the easiest. It's -- if you look at the top, the numbers, it's 0211-7022. Yep.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We couldn't hear the surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the surname for the interpreter, Judge?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Tekic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is this a statement made to an authorised official of the Banja Luka CSB, and it says regarding his stay in Teslic. And he says: "I'm not a member of any military formation. I arrived Teslic at the beginning of July of this year as a member of the group sent by the Doboj CSB, or more precisely, by Chief Bjelosevic and his deputy, Savic, in order to restore order and discipline in the police and town." Now, from your inquiries into this case, Judge Peric, the statement that he was sent by Andrija Bjelosevic and his deputy, Milan Savic is that something that was confirmed by other evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I do not think so. As far as I can recall, they all had official police IDs and in the final analysis it would be strange to have Andrija Bjelosevic to be sending civilians together with the police to Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Again, from your investigations into this matter, what role did you conclude had been played by Bjelosevic and Milan Savic, his deputy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: According to what we have determined in the course of the investigation, they were the ones who had organised the group, who sent them to Teslic, and gave them authorisation. I think all of them had official IDs, military uniforms, weapons. I don't think there was one single exception to this. There were even people in that group, among them a man I knew from before the war, who was a police -- who had been a police inspector in Brod before that, but there were also people who were criminals who had had criminal records. I knew one of them as well, so I was astonished to see that they were part of the police group. They were certainly organised by Andrija Bjelosevic and Savic. We determined that during the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm a little bit puzzled. Is this answer not directly in contradiction with the previous one and, if so, could you clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think it may be the way I asked the question originally that wasn't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I think in -- it's page 27, line 17, starting with Ms. Korner, I think it should be deleted -- not deleted but to make another line but there is no mention that Judge Delvoie posed that question in line 17, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Your Honours' intervention hasn't been recorded at all in the transcript. It may be because he was still speaking and I over-spoke or you over-spoke. It's quite difficult with the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, can I just ask you this: My original question when we were reading the statement of this chap, Tekic, was to you, did you conclude that what he -- I have to look at my own question, I suppose. I asked you whether the statement made by Tekic, that he been sent by Andrija Bjelosevic and his deputy Milan Savic, is something that was confirmed by other evidence. And you said I don't think so. As far as can I recall they all had official police IDs, and in the final analysis it would be strange to have Andrija Bjelosevic to be sending civilians together with the police. And then you said later in answer the question I then asked you, what role did you conclude had been played by Bjelosevic and Savic, was that they effectively had organised all of this and sent the Mice. And there is an apparent contradiction between those two answers. Could you just explain? As I say, it may be the way I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I do not see any contradiction. This man was a member of a police formation that was organised, that was set up by this Bjelosevic. Both of my answers point to that. So Tekic was part of a formation. Here it's stated military but it was a police formation. He arrived armed, together with this group, with police ID. He told us that he had been sent by Bjelosevic and Milan Savic. So they couldn't have been sent to Teslic without having received an assignment, a police assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your original answer meant -- it was dealing with the fact that this civilian should not have had -- if he was a civilian and not a member of the police, should not have had a police identification card supplied by Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: That was my conclusion; namely, that he couldn't have been a civilian, that he must have been a member of reserve of police forces, who was mobilized back into the police, armed, and sent to Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I had never come across a situation where police would issue weapons, IDs, uniforms without that person being either part of the reserve police or someone with an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if you're about to move on, it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am, yes -- well, I'm still on the same topic, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Judge Peric, we are at the point where we would take our first break. The Court will rise now, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If we could go into closed session before the -- we resume the testimony of the witness. Private session, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, sorry about that small digression?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to continue on the theme for a moment on the responsibility for bringing the Mice to Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In 1999, after the discovery of the bodies of victims of the Mice's activities, I think there was flurry of publicity and articles in a number of different newspapers within Bosnia and the Republika Srpska. In one of them you gave an interview, and that was to "Nezavisne Novine"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in the course of that interview, and I want to ask you about this part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not seeking to put the interview in, but it's at tab 56 of Your Honours' bundles or whatever, and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said this: "When I told Municipal President Nikola Perisic that he would pay for these crimes sooner or later, he just smiled naively believing that no one would be responsible." First, did you -- did you say that to the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From your investigations, what role did you conclude that President -- municipal President Perisic had played in -- in this scenario of the Mice coming to Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: My conclusion was that his role was crucial, both in bringing them over, as well, I believe, in what they did in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in what way "crucial"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, he was the president of the municipality. He was in charge of the Crisis Staff, at its head. He was the one who influenced and had the crucial role in adopting the decisions by -- by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And how -- how did -- sorry. How did that impact on -- on -- on the bringing to Teslic of the Mice?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: The decision to bring them was adopted by the Crisis Staff. Based on that decision, two people went to Doboj to arrange their arrival. They spoke to Andrija Bjelosevic and Ljubisa Petricevic. We found that out during the investigation. I believed that Vid Stojanovic [phoen], too, who took part in those talks was interviewed during the investigation, so I believe it was him who spoke about that. It was my conclusion that Nikola Perisic had the -- played the key, crucial role. He was the kind of man who wanted to have the main say in all things military and civilian, and, hence, his arguments and strife with many people. There was him on one side and on the other side were the military structures of both Doboj and Teslic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this file of the Mice it contains Official Notes made by the head of the police in the SJB in Teslic, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may I just --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: A small question. The witness said two people went to Doboj to ask for assistance and to ask the Mice Group to come in. Who were those two people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, did you hear the question? Who were the two people who went to Doboj?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: One was Bosko Misic, a people's deputy, and the other was the chief of All People's Defence, his name was Vid Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To return to what I was asking you, this file contains statements made by the chief of the SJB in Teslic, Mr. Kuzmanovic. And also by the commander, Mr. Markovic. From your investigations, what did you conclude about the police's attitude in Teslic, those who were already there, the SJB heads, in respect of the Mice?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: What we were able to conclude was that -- that they had accepted the Mice and surrendered all police authority to them. They really had no influence over that group. I would dare to call that the suspension of authority of the local police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. At that stage, when the -- sorry. Go on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that they only serviced certain people with information about some operations they planned and so on. So they were not completely marginalised. They had a certain role, they met them daily, there was communication and contact, but during that period, I believe that it was the Mice who were the sole decision-makers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At that stage, when the Mice came in at the beginning of June 1992, roughly how many active and reserve police officers were there in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think there were about 200 to 300 of them. I don't know a precise figure, but certainly more than 200.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kuzmanovic and Mr. Markovic, when Predrag Radulovic came in, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: After that operation, they were removed from their positions. I believe that they were discharged from the police. Possibly they were employed by the Doboj police. I don't remember anymore. Temporarily people from Banja Luka had taken over the positions of chief and commander of police, and the chief of the crime investigation department. After that, another man was appointed chief of police. I believe his name was Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know -- because the Court has seen documents complaining about them -- the -- Mr. Markovic and Mr. Kuzmanovic being reinstated. Do you know if they were reinstated at any stage; in other words, went back to the SJB in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that they returned to the police structures, and I know that there was a problem with that at the political level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what sort of problem was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: There was no agreement about their return. In the military structures, and I believe in political circles, there was opposition because they were not in the same political party. Markovic was a radical whereas Perisic was a member of the SDS, and there was some sort of conflict that arose over that, between them. Perisic did not agree with their return, which was imposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And, again, from your investigations, you've talked about effectively military police and political cooperation on this. What was the purpose of this whole operation, of bringing in the Mice into Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I can only assume what it was about. I didn't see any real need for people to come in from outside for purposes of mobilisation as it had been put in their statements. They said that they been called in to assist in the mobilisation process. I wasn't aware of any problems related to that. So my conclusion was that they had come to create an atmosphere of fear and, thus, exert pressure to bring about voluntary departures and removal. That may not have been the original objective but to my mind, this was exactly their role. For some 20 day, their activity was tolerated until Nikola Perisic risked being arrested himself. There was even talk about killing him. So I believe that what ensued was a consequence of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it may -- obviously it may be obvious, but who was it that they were trying to bring about the voluntary departure of? What sections of the population.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: The Bosniaks and Croats. Finally, two operations of the so-called cleansing of those villages were a implementation of that idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just finish the -- with the -- the topic of the Mice. I mean, the Court has heard a fair amount about it. Can we look next please at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, there is just one little problem or question that I would wish to kick in, namely, in relation to the witness's explanation that the reinstatement of Markovic and the other guy was imposed. And my question would be imposed by whom. It's in page 35, line 25 in the transcript on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, did you hear the question from Judge Harhoff. You said that the reinstatement of Markovic and, Kuzmanovic, I think it is, was imposed. And the question is: By whom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think it was the police structures and military structures from Doboj who imposed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I have a small question to, if you want, as we are leaving the topic of the Mice now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're not, Your Honour. I'm going through some of the things that happened, but certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, that's okay. Then I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if you like, why don't you ask now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness said - and this is, if I'm not wrong, not in his prior statement - that he was at a meeting in Banja Luka when Perisic and someone else came to ask to do something about the Mice Group. My question is: How did it came about that he was there; and what was discussed there? What was ... what was the purpose -- the purpose and the content of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour is quite right. I skipped rather over that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, you told us you do now remember, you had been asked about this before, and you said you couldn't remember, but you now recall going to a meeting in Banja Luka together with Perisic and, I think, the judge at the Teslic court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Perisic was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was the judge of the Teslic court also with you, whose name - I apologise - I --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, the president of the court also came with me. I think that Predrag Radulovic insisted that we go to tell Mr. Zupljanin about the situation. That was our only role to confirm what Radulovic, I suppose, had earlier informed Mr. Zupljanin about as a problem. And as far as I remember, the conversation was only about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who suggested the meeting, that you go? Mr. Radulovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Radulovic. I cannot be certain, but I think that he invited us. We took some small roads for safety reasons --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: -- my conclusion was that it was his idea and his plan, that he was the organiser.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you -- at the meeting, when you -- did you -- did you speak to Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the details of the conversation. There was several people. I'm not sure who presented the situation or what I said. I don't remember that. I remember that there were people from the corps, the military. Then people from military security. There was the President of the Banja Luka court and the prosecutor from the Banja Luka prosecutor's office. So several people were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you know a Colonel Stevilovic from the 1st Krajina Corps, the intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that he attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what about a gentleman named Nedeljko Kesic, head of the SNB in Banja Luka. Was he there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Nedeljko Kesic, yes, I believe that he was there. I'm almost certain that he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, I can see that it's not something that you remember that clearly. But can you remember how matters were left at the end of the meeting; in other words, was anything said to you by Mr. Zupljanin that he would help, or wouldn't help, or what would happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that any decision was communicated to us then. I suppose that the decision was taken after the meeting. I cannot confirm that though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That's all I want to ask. All right. Can we just move through quickly the documents that show what happened in this case. Could you have a look, please, at your tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's P837.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the report to the investigating judge in Teslic, which was -- went out under Mr. Radulovic's name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that -- is that the sort of standard report that would come from the police when they had made arrests for crimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is a very bad copy and we'll see the names more clearly later on, but at no stage does it appear that Milan Savic was ever arrested; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Really, he wasn't covered by this criminal report, and he was not apprehended. I checked that in the meantime. I mistakenly believed that he was in hospital because one of the Mice was so badly beaten up that he was in hospital rather than in detention. But it was for Dobrivoje Culibrk, but Milan Savic wasn't affected by this operation and he was not apprehended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know why that was? Did you ever make inquiries as to why Milan Savic, who everybody said was in charge of all of this, or part of it, was never arrested or interviewed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I cannot explain that. Predrag Radulovic probably knows that. Both were state security men. I suppose that it has to do with their relations. Ljubisa Petricevic wasn't arrested either, although he was also involved. Allegedly, however, the military police apprehended him and took him to Banja Luka and I don't know what happened later, but he wasn't covered by this criminal report either. The two of them were omitted by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll see in a moment the documents from the military and police side requesting the release of various people. From what your experience of what happened then and what was happening, could the military and police structures have had any bearing on the fact that the two leaders weren't arrested? Any influence, I should say, really.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then look, please, at document, next tab for you, 168, P703 for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. This is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Ms. Korner. It's just a correction to the transcript. Page 39, line 16, instead of "alleged him" should be "arrested him."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is -- it starts off. It's a report, again, from Mr. Radulovic, who is at this time is temporary chief of Teslic SJB, and he says about 40 Muslims and Croats have been massacred in the Teslic municipality by a group of criminals from Doboj. And then he goes on to say that there was damage, rape, amongst girls and women of all nationalities, which has caused fear among the citizens. First of all, is that right, that effectively it wasn't just non-Serbs who were frightened, it was also Serbs, by the activities of this group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: That is correct. A very significant number of Serbs was affected by their activities of robbery, stealing cars, and the like. There were even allegations of rape, although I never got any hard evidence about -- about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And he is asking, it says on the basis of an agreement with political bodies in Teslic, representatives of the army, the president, and the lower court - this is the third paragraph - and the public prosecutor, it was decided that an exhumation be conducted of the 40 people who had been killed. And -- he asked for a forensic team. Now, was any kind of an exhumation conducted then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I made a proposal to the investigating judge to conduct an exhumation and he decided in favour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But did he --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: The cost of the exhumation should be covered from the budget. But there the problem arose. The minister of justice, I believe, told the President of the court that the government had no Monday for that and that it must wait; that for the government this was financial problem. Radulovic, however, exaggerates here there. There has never been -- there had never been talks with the politicians about the exhumation. That was an exclusively -- that was under the exclusive jurisdiction of the court, and we never spoke to politicians about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the minister of justice in July, was that Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, whether it was Momcilo Mandic or -- or whether it was Ostojic. The president of the court would know that better. I got the information from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I don't think we need -- we've got a criminal report but you've seen that. Because of time, that's the next -- then there's a further request from -- I think -- we can skip that one, actually. Yes, can we look, please, at document at your tab 20, P1312, please, just for a moment. This is the decision of the investigating judge, Mr. Kovacevic, who -- the person you mentioned went to this meeting in Banja Luka, saying that the investigation should be carried out. Is that an order to the -- to you or to the police, or to both of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: It's a decision of the investigating judge to accept the prosecutor's application and provided the evidence applied for. So this is merely the decision to launch an investigation and an acceptance of the prosecutor's application. It refers exclusively to what the prosecutor had applied for.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And now can we look, please, at another report, which is at your tab 21, and it's 2837. You told -- this is a report by Milos, which I don't imagine you saw before you were asked to look through various documents. But in the first paragraph, he's talking about the overall trend in the broader area of Doboj. Two currents in the SDS party: One is more moderate and has a relatively realistic human and rational stand on the issue of the resolution of issues of ethnic groups living in areas where the Serbs are a majority; the second current, which has currently been able to impose itself more in certain areas, is developing the idea of an ethnically cleansed environment, republic of -- ethnically cleansed Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina and is acting in keeping with this by not hesitating to resort to whatever means to attain this goal. And then it goes on to say that the killing of civilians in Doboj, Teslic, and Kozarac are not in favour of Serbian dignity and the honour of the Serbian army and so on. Does this report, as it were, go with what you have just told the Court about the reason that the Mice came into Teslic, that what was proposed here or what is stated here is that there was a strain of the SDS that wanted an ethnically cleansed Serbian republic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether we can speak about two strains within the SDS, but there certainly were extremist individuals in the SDS and there were some in Teslic. One of them was Sava Knezevic, a public deputy and an Orthodox priest. So these extreme trends were not at all alien to us; they were not abstract. But on the whole, within the party, I don't think that there were two groups that significantly differed in their political attitudes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So over all, this say there are two groups, one that wants to ethnically cleanse, one that is more moderate on the issue of ethnic groups other than Serbs living in -- in these areas. How, from your experience, would you have put the overall aim of the SDS in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that the policy of the SDS essentially boiled down to ethnic cleansing and that the extreme current, to call it that conditionally, was able to assert itself in the SDS. And it was finally implemented, and that was the result of this policy during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that -- are you now talking about just Teslic or overall?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Teslic because I'm familiar with the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. All right. Now can we move, please -- well, let's just ... sorry. I just want to check ... Yes. Can you just look, please, for a moment at document 10362, your tab 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I'm not seeking to make this an exhibit because it is not on our 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I think you have had a chance to look at it. It's a long description from the military point of view, 1st Krajina Corps effectively, of the -- the Mice and the Teslic [sic]. Can you turn to the -- yes, it's the second page in B/C/S and it's the third page in English. There's -- is it up? No, third page?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says in the third para: "Aside from the same individuals," that's Petricevic and the others, "committed several threats, blackmail, robberies, and rapes and up until now it has been confirmed that it's been around 80.500 Deutschemarks, et cetera, as well larger amounts of gold and luxurious cars were taken from certain persons and citizens of Teslic. Those are fairly high figures. From your investigations, are those figures reasonably accurate?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I believe that the figures were mentioned in the course ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then it says in the next paragraph: "On the 1st of July, information about the situation in the area of Teslic municipality was put together which was then sent by General Talic to Mr. Karadzic with specific suggestions on measures to be taken." Now, were you aware that a report went all the way up to Mr. Karadzic, apparently, on this matter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware. But I assumed that Karadzic did have such information from several sources. I am sure that Karadzic must have known about the events, but I did not know about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why do you say you're sure that Mr. Karadzic must have known about these events?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Because he had his deputies, people's deputies, who were also members of the Main Board of the SDS. He was at the head of the Main Board. I think they were exchanging such information. I simply believed it couldn't have remained a secret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's all I want to ask you about that document. Could you look now, please, at -- it's already an Exhibit. No -- yes, can we look at the two requests for release, please, first one at your tab 25, 3571 -- 65 ter 3571. The -- this is to the -- from the Operations Group Command at Doboj to Teslic investigating judge, asking for the release, immediate release so they can take part in combat operations. And all of those men, I think, if -- the document we looked at, the report, Mr. Sljuka was number 9, Mr. Sljivic number 8, Gavranovic number 13, Kezunovic is number 14, Momic 12, Slavuljica, whatever, they are all on the list anyhow. Did you see this request at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The investigative judge did show me the request, because, at the time, we had some other information -- or, rather, threats from Doboj, lawyers from Doboj who were representing some of the persons mentioned here openly told us that we are living dangerously, that Teslic will be bombarded from Ozren mountain, so that because of the verbal threats we paid more attention to this very document as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Had had happened before, that there had been a request from military officials, senior military officers for the release of people who had been lawfully arrested for criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: We haven't had cases of pressure excerpted by the army in other cases. There was one case when the president of the municipality, Mr. Perisic, asked a group of people from a village to ask us to release one of the people from the village, but never from the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that please be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we look, please, at your document 27, tab 27, it's already exhibited, 1342 -- P1342, sorry, not the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Same kind of request by Mr. Bjelosevic. Again, was this something that the investigating -- in fact, I think dated exactly the same day, yes, both of them dated the 17th of July. Again, did Mr. President Kovacevic show you this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I -- I am aware of this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you requests from senior officers, police officers before, to have members of the police who had been -- or alleged police who had been lawfully arrested, released?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No. We never had that kind of pressure exerted by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. And just hopefully to go through this a bit more quickly now. I think that, if we look, please, at P1314, Exhibit P1314. And it's the next tab for you, Judge, at tab 28. This is the President of the Doboj High Court, Mr. Neskovic, who is saying that the individuals who had been sent to Banja Luka prison, I think, should be transferred to Doboj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why had they originally been sent to Banja Luka prison?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Because in our assessment, their stay in Doboj could have obstructed the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind how these people arrived. And, therefore, it was arranged with the warden of the Banja Luka prison for them to be accommodated in Banja Luka, although the Banja Luka prison, according to the prison system, people from Teslic shouldn't have been sent to Banja Luka, but I think it was the investigative judge who held talks in relation to this issue and, eventually, these people were accommodated in the District Prison in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as a result of this order by Mr. -- by Judge Neskovic were they, in fact, transferred to Doboj?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to this fax, they were transferred to Doboj. We found out about their transfer from the media or maybe someone informed us about it. And then, at least I believe we went to the president of the high court in Banja Luka who told us that he knows nothing about that and later on told us that, after having asked a prison warden in Banja Luka, that they were actually released on the basis of this fax. So it was even without the knowledge of the President of the High Court which was the supervisory organ that these people were transferred to Doboj. That's the information we received. But this fax was addressed, as we can see here, to the president of the high court in Banja Luka which leads me to believe that he must have known about the request and approved of it, at least verbally, if not in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then I think it's right, we can deal with that quite quickly, that they were, in fact, released by Judge Neskovic; is that right? He ordered their release?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we look very quickly at the next document because it's s already an exhibit. That's P1353.09, your tab 30. As you say, this received a great deal of publicity or -- probably it's because there's a long article in "Glas" headed: "The notorious Mice are free." Now, I said there was a great deal. Was there, in fact, publicity not only in "Glas" but in other newspapers about the release of these men?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether other media covered it as well, because, at the time, I think "Glas" was the only local media that reached Teslic. I haven't noticed any publicity elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
