utterances.text: All right. As a matter of interest, can I just ask you, did you know anything about "Glas"? In other words, its relationship to the SDS and the -- and the government of the Serbian Republic? If you didn't, say so.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I believe they were -- these were all newspapers of the SDS. There were no independent newspapers until after the war. Media were controlled by the SDS; let me put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. When we look at your log-book, the Teslic log-book, we'll just look at the Mice then. But that's the end of, I think, all that I want to ask you about -- let me just check, if I may, on my note. Well, yes, I think when you saw the investigator and the lawyer in Banja Luka you had a look -- you looked at the Doboj register for the prison, is that right, and you were able to identify the names of the people in -- in the Doboj prison. Do you remember that? When you were seen a few weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think it's self-evident. So don't worry, Judge. It's my fault. Now, can I just deal before we look at the log-books with a couple of other matters. You've mentioned now and again the attacks on the -- or the disarming operations, perhaps that's a better way of putting it, on the villages of Stenjak and Rankovici, and you talked about that in your interview at pages 71 and following. I want to show you a couple of documents in relation to those. Is that right -- you told us -- you told the OTP in your interviews that these disarmament operations took place shortly after the Mice arrived, around the 8th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think the first operation was Stenjak; and then, on the 8th of June, Rankovici, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the population of those villages, what was that -- what nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Bosniaks, or Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you -- yes. Can I ask you to look, please, at a record of an exhumation that was done a great deal later, in 1999, which is, please, at your tab 41. And it's document 65 ter 2517. And in English, can we go to the seventh page; and in the -- in the B/C/S version -- just a moment. I'm sorry, I forgot to mark that. It will be at the bottom of -- it starts at the bottom of page 3, paragraph 2 or whatever. It's up. Thank you. It says: "The first grave which we began the planned exhumation work in the Bosniak cemetery of Stenjak," and it describes where it is. "According to preliminary information, staging an attack by the Bosniaks, the Teslic Serbs in fact attacked the Bosniaks in the village of Stenjak between the 3 and 10 June 1992" -- Sorry, we need to go to the next page, I think, of this in -- in B/C/S. And "killed about 17 unarmed Bosniak civilians whose bodies were collected in the village much later ..." And then, [indiscernible]. Did -- from your understanding at the time, were unarmed people killed during the operation at Stenjak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I cannot give any comment on that, because I don't know what the outcome of the operations were in relation to civilians, whether they were armed or unarmed people. I have no first-hand information. I don't even know about them. I've never heard about this mass grave in Stenjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you this: What was your understanding then of the purpose of the operations that were carried out against Stenjak and Gornji Rankovici?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think the purpose was to mop up or cleanse the settlements, and it was a part of a plan. In the final analysis, the same was happening to the Serbian villages on the other side, so some of the people who fled from there were accommodated in Stenjak and Rankovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just check one other document on this topic, and then I want to ask you about your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, now, I don't think, in light of your answers, I can ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we now look, please, at the report you told us you compiled and which is part of your 65 ter package. It is it -- in fact, it has been exhibited before, P1353.15. Sorry, it's tab 84 for you, Judge. Was this report prepared by you for a meeting of the Municipal Assembly in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did -- I did do -- I did do prepare this report. It was sent to the municipality. It was a report. I think they were legally bound to inform the parliament about trends related to crimes or perpetration of crimes. I took the opportunity to inform the politicians about the situation regarding the crime. The report show what my information was and what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at paragraph 3, after you deal with the statistics of what happened. You look -- you set out something a paragraph headed: "Actual Crime Situation." And you said: "Recorded crime is a refraction of the real crime existing in society today. Most criminal acts remain undiscovered and many crimes are tolerated by the authorities for various reasons. The prosecutor's office has knowledge of day-to-day looting of property, houses, and business premises being set on fire and destroyed. Armed robbery and murder being committed for base motives, socially owned flats and private houses being occupied unlawfully, the stealing of forest timber, and other forms of wilful acts. There is no criminal prosecution for most of these acts. In ten days alone, there were three murders for base motives and several cases of arson and armed robbery. In only one cases were the perpetrators arrested and criminal proceedings initiated against them. The perpetrators of the other two murders have not been arrested to the present day. Public prosecutor and the president of the court personally demanded that the command of the Teslic Serbian Brigade arrest one accomplice on suspicion of murder. It is inexplicable why these people have not been arrested." And is that what you were speaking about earlier, Judge, when you said that the police were not - and I'm summarizing - carrying out their properly? Sorry, did you hear the question? Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely that. A large number of crimes that even the public knew about and about which we had information were not processed by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say this: "The destruction of religious buildings is a war crime against civilians because of the way and the circumstances in which it was perpetrated. The Serbian people will carry a heavy burden of historical responsibility until the perpetrators of these and similar criminal acts are brought to justice." Is that a view that you held at the time and still hold today?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Of course. As can you see, I was trying to warn, inform people in the political leadership, people in the power that these were war crimes. I was telling that to various people like that, both privately and at meeting and from this, you can see what -- how I viewed these type of crimes. I could not explain. I could not see how it is possible for religious facilities to be destroyed and then no criminal report to reach us and to have police simply remain silent about it. And my conclusions were that this was done with the approval of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "The state and its law enforcement organs must urgently answer the following question: What are the causes of these serious crimes and why are they not being disclosed? An answer to this question should be sought from the command of the Teslic Serbian Brigade and interior ministry organs. Otherwise, the impression will be created that this state of crime in the army ranks is tolerated and that no one tries to prevent it, whilst the interior ministry organs will be placed in an unenviable professional situation." And then you go on to suggest whatever it is. And you talked about the religious destruction that you personally knew about in your interview, and I'm not going to ask you about that again. Now, finally, Judge, can I deal with the log-books that were maintained at the Teslic court and about which you were asked to provide various statistics, and we're going to look at some of the cases. Were you able to -- you provided the statistics, we made a note, and we sent you a copy translated of that note.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the one that appears at the end of the proofing note headed: "Statistical Data from the Teslic Log-Books."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are able to confirm that those figures are accurate?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I perused this register and my assumption is that the figures are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going to go through some of the entries in the KT book. So, first of all, I think you were able to confirm that between April -- or you gave us the figures between the 1st of April and the 31st of December, 1992 the police -- the police submitted to the basic prosecutor's office in Teslic criminal reports against 395 people. And for approximately ten of these cases, it's impossible to determine that the originator was the police, because the remarks in the book state they were transferred from other log-books; that is to say, the KTA which is the -- effectively the file which keeps documents, which relate to potential cases; and the KTN, which records unknown perpetrators. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, according to the KT log-book, 1992 to 1993, the police filed criminal reports in seven cases during 1992 and no cases in 1993 for crimes committed between the 1st of April and the 31st of December, 1992 by Serb perpetrators where the aggrieved parties were Muslims or Croats. So only seven cases all together. And I think we better look at those cases in a little detail, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we have up the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've got in front of you I think your -- your KTN -- your KT book. And the -- it's right at the end. I think we need to have up first 0 -- 65 ter 1546. And it's tab -- sorry. No, it's not tab -- it won't be a tab. You should have the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's got the whole book. Yeah. And now I need to get it. Will Your Honours forgive me for a moment while I just get the copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now the first case, could we look at is, at -- it's number 126 in the register. And it's -- it should be on page 05049809 in the original B/C/S. Now, we can -- if we can get the right pages up for -- it's the first page in the English translation. Sorry, this is not -- this is actually cases of -- I'm doing the whole book, actually, because it's easier that way. We'll come to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 100?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at entry 126. Sorry, I just want to look at some of the cases of armed rebellion as well. While we're at it, we'll do the whole book together.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, Rifan Sakic was reported, criminal offence under Articles 119 and 124. Those are two offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, and, Your Honours, I do have, as part of the law library, which seems to go ever further back in being produced. But that is of the -- the old Yugoslav law, is it not, and Article 119 is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think that the offences in question are armed rebellion and serving in an enemy army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. Okay. So let's just look at those. We see there that there were three people, is that right -- no, more than that. Three -- if we go to page 3 of the English --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- 4 of the English, rather. We'll see that some --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Six persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- six persons charged with armed rebellion and serving in the enemy's forces, which is 119. And does the log show what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: It should show a request to launch an investigation. Now this says "ceded." Ceded to the higher. Probably higher prosecutor's office. Hmm, let me check. I can't really find my way in these log-books.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Don't worry. I don't think it matters much anyhow. So that's the first case of armed rebellion. I should have -- fax said that the book show all together, and you checked, there is a total of 20 persons being reported for armed rebellion. The next one that -- can we go to is 120 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, since you're about to go on to a new book, perhaps we should take the break at this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not, I'm just going straight through this book, but I'm going through the entries that are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I would alert you that, according to our calculations, you have about 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm going deal with the entries in the book, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, can we go on with the -- can we go on as quickly as we can because I have very little time left with the log-book. Number 127 which you will find on page -- it's the fourth page in the English translation and in the B/C/S it's got 05049811. Which is page 6. 127, we've got a number of Muslims, is that right, apparently from the Gornji Rankovic operation, who were charged under Article 213, this time of the Bosnian Criminal Code, and I think we'll find that's illegal possession of weapons.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then can we move, 148, which you will find on page 6 -- sorry, the English, but it's 05049817 in B/C/S, which is page 12 in -- in the actual log-book charged under the SFRY code with Article 124.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: SFRJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Which is armed rebellion again. I should say that you -- the statistics you worked out for armed rebellion cases were a total of -- sorry. Forgive me, I have lost my sheet of paper with those figures on it, which is very unhelpful of me. 20 persons all together?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we go, please, because there's a lot of people involved in this one, it goes on for pages, to entry number 149 in the log, 10th of July, 05049825. It's page 14 in English and page 20 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is one of the ones where Serbs were charged. And I think here we see, is this right, the Mice? Entry 149.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You should have at the top, page 05049825 stamped. It's page 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, 149. Correct. It's about the Mice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I can't see if it is up on the screen. It is. Right. They're charged with a number of different offences. I think 52 is under the Bosnian Code false imprisonment, 151 is robbery, 148 is aggravated theft, and 160 is extortion and murder. Now, if we go, please, in the next page in English, and I think to the next page in -- we see it goes on and on and on. Does the file show that in fact there was no criminal proceedings at all against any of these men, were actually brought to any conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: You mean with regard to the Mice?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. So far, none has been concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are the people who were charged and recorded in this book still at large? In other words, are they still wondering the streets?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, they're at large. I think that proceedings were launched only against one. But, no, he was -- he belonged to -- he didn't belong to the Mice; he was from the Teslic police. No other criminal proceedings were launched against the Mice anywhere, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move to the second book, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to ask that both books be exhibited together. I mean, they've been translated together. So it's page 20 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Second book for you, and can we go for you to 157. And it's page 05 -- 05049625 is stamped at the top. It's 28 in the B/C/S. Now, again, this is one of the seven examples you found of a Serb being charged in relation to an offence apparently committed against a Muslim. And I think 148 is the charge of aggravated theft? Do you remember anything about the details of this case?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this was a group of three or four persons who had committed several criminal offences of aggravated theft in several areas. I think that there were both Serbs and Muslims among the victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, as the harmed party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then can we go to 160. It's on the same page in the English. I think it may be in the same page in the B/C/S. It is. Again, is that a case where Serbs, a number of them, were charged with -- with murder. And this time defamation. Do you remember about that case? This is a whole group. The one before that was a single one. 160, there are four of them it looks like?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No, I spoke about a number 160. And which one were you referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 157. Somebody called Mile Stanojevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is also about aggravated theft.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So the one you were talking about was the one involving four. If we look at the result for each of these cases, we need to go to the next page in English, page 21, we see that in respect of Mr. Stanojevic, the investigation appears to have been terminated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I can't find the box.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the box, I think, 46.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes this is what it says: "Investigation terminated," as a remark. Yes, the remark is that the investigation was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And for the other, the group one, does it look -- they were given although they were sentenced apparently in 1998, nothing happened until then. They were given an amnesty?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I can't explain what happened. Obviously, this was after I was relieved of my duties. So I don't know the outcome. It is possible, since this involves persons who were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Members of military units, they may have gone to battle-fields and were not available throughout the war. This could happen, and we did have such problems who -- with people who committed crimes and, due to the war operations, we could not get at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if they were soldiers, then why were they dealt with by the civilian court? This is in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Possibly the military court didn't function in that period either. We launched these proceedings because we thought that we were more efficient and that there would be no objections based on jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move then, please, as quickly as we can to 166 in your book, page 22 in English, 05049627 in the original, page 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's page -- sorry, Judge, when I say 30 it's our purposes, not yours. You need to look at the number at the top.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Which entry?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 166, 15th of September, 1992. The perpetrators appear to be Serbs, and indeed there seems to be a woman with them, Natasa Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the victim is Muharem Demir, charged, amongst other things, with aggravated theft. Are you able to confirm whether the facts were that these -- they broke into the garage of a non-Serb and stole a bicycle?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is theft. Mostly these are -- these instances of breaking and entering.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is right that it shows here that the proceedings were suspended under column 29?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, unfortunately it's gone slightly odd in the translation, but I think the original does show that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I can't see it in the log-book here, so I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm told I've got very little time left, so we need to really go through this at speed. 170?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, very quickly, and I think I will just have to list the other ones because we won't have enough time. At 170, do we see further people charged -- which is page 24 in English; 05049629 in your copy.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Bruno Pajunovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Further armed rebellion case against -- is this right? Are they Croats here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are the Croats from the village of Slatina and the other village is Donja Komusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is another armed rebellion at 173. Can we go to 178, please, page 28 in English and it's 36 in B/C/S for the e-court. But it's page 05049633 for you. Is that again a case where a Serb was charged but the victim was a Muslim. And does the charge show in 153 is --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- that a -- is that theft of a car?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think so. Yes. Stealing a car. Probably this is a stolen passenger car.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then 182, please, at page 30; 05049635. 3rd of November. Is that, again, a Serb perpetrator? Doesn't actually show the victim.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Entry 182, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. And does that -- it is illegible in our copy that's why it has not been translated. Does it, in fact, show that the victim was a Muslim? Are you able to read it? Apparently the translator couldn't.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Judging by the surname, Hadzijusic [phoen] or something, I can't really tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, as I say, I'm going have to list the rest. Except 185, I think we'll see slightly more serious. Page 32 in English, 05049637, and it's page 40 for the e-court, B/C/S. Again, was that a Serb perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And -- and a Muslim victim?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: The victim was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Bosniak. And was this, in fact, a house fire, and the charge was of that endangering public safety.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't think we've got enough time to go through the other entries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the cases of, just for the purposes of the record, [indiscernible] of Serb perpetrators, are those which are listed as entries or the ones we've been through, 149, 157, 160, 166, 178, 182, and 185. And as I've said already, the statistics as confirmed by Judge Peric are that in the KT log-book a total of 20 persons reported for the crime of armed insurrection, Article 124, in 1992; one person in 1993; 81 persons reported for the crime of service in the enemy army, Article 119 in 1992; and four persons in 1993 for the crimes committed in 1992. Then I think a total of 92 persons were reported for illegal possession of fire-arms, Article 213 in 1992 and 24 persons in 1993, but the crime is committed in 1992. And according to the KTN log-book, the police filed criminal reports against 21 unknown perpetrators in 1992. Five unknown perpetrators in 1993 for crimes committed in 1992. And in six of the unknown perpetrator cases reported in 1992, the victim was a non-Serb. And only two of the unknown perpetrator cases reported in 1993 was the victim -- again, crimes committed in 1992, was the victim a non-Serb. No criminal charges against Serbs for war crimes committed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And those are the statistics you found from going through the books, are they, Judge Peric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I perused all the log-books and the result was as we've seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask that the two KT books -- registers, rather, should be exhibited together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01365. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally, Judge Peric, this. We've seen that there -- there are some cases where there were Serb perpetrators and it involved non-Serb victims where there prosecutions, investigations and prosecutions. Are you able to say why that was? I mean, the crimes that we've seen are, I suppose, in terms of what you've described happening in Teslic in your report much less, but why were these people prosecuted and others not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think that the people processed were criminals of classical type so to speak, and in the case where the people weren't prosecuted, those were the people either that were under the control of the police or the case was that maybe police didn't want them to be prosecuted. That's the only conclusion I can reach.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, indeed Judge. That's all I ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before you complete your examination-in-chief, I just sat with one question in relation to the entry that you showed to Judge Peric in respect of the persons who were not prosecuted in 1992 or 1993 but finally were prosecuted and sentenced in 1998 and then subsequently given an amnesty. And my question was, and I apologise for not having picked it up while Judge Peric was giving his testimony, but my question is whether these people who were finally sentenced in 1998 and subsequently given an amnesty were members of the Mice Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's entry 160, Your Honour, at page 20 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Judge, if can you go back to that, 05049625 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You don't have to do that. Just let me confirm with Judge Peric that, indeed, these people who were not prosecuted in 1992 or 1993 but were finally prosecuted in 1998, and then subsequently given an amnesty, that they were indeed members of the Mice Group. Judge can you confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, were these people at 160, were they members of the Mice Group? Maybe they were actually. I have to go back to the name.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No. The men under 160 were not members of the Mice. This is a group of criminals who were registered as habitual offenders. So common criminals. They were not in any way related to the Mice Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you again, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Peric, good day to you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Cvijetic. I represent, among others, Mr. Mico Stanisic, the accused here. Before we start discussing specific issues, I would like to start by asking you a few questions concerning your appointment to the position of public prosecutor. Could you please tell us, based on which decision by which organ you became the public prosecutor in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: It was a specific situation. It was not according to the law. I left Brod on the 3rd or the 4th of March, because I lived in Bosanski Brod, and with the start of the war, I moved to Teslic, because I was born in the surroundings of Teslic. And at about 20th of May a prosecutor from Teslic left and the prosecutor's office was left without a prosecutor. The president of the executive board who knew me and who knew that I was in Teslic asked me to take over this position. He explained that the institution suddenly didn't have a prosecutor and that the government need to do something about it. He asked -- he told me that they would make an appointment and that he will arrange it with the parliament that the parliament later approves of my appointment. So it was on the basis of a decision by the Executive Board that I became the prosecutor there. I don't know whether I was also given some kind of work obligation or assigned a work assignment, because everyone in Teslic did have. But I was appointed based on a decision by the Executive Board, and I was appointed only later, in August, by the National Assembly and according to the legal procedure at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It was a situation that was not in keeping with the law and that was forced by the circumstances of Teslic at the time. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this and what I mean by it is that there was no communication with a central authority. Are you -- do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: What central organs do you refer to? We did have communications with Banja Luka and with Pale, but the connection with -- the communication with Doboj, I think, at the time, was not functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I can show you a document and then we can elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask for 1D03-3322 to be put on the screen. 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Peric. Do you have the registrator [as interpreted]? It's in this binder, can you find it under 35?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: What we have here is a 1996 document. It's a decision on the termination of my post.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just give us a moment. We'll try and find it. I don't think we've -- it's the right document in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can counsel please repeat the number again, please. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D03-3322.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I think that we have the right document now. Mr. Peric, in this document, we can see it's a decision stating that your employment in the public prosecutor's office is terminated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in the statement of reasons, we can see that you were appointed on the 21st of May, 1992, by the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph of the statement of reason, one can read that the National Assembly, at its session of 14 June 1995, adopted a decision relieving you of this duty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And below that, you can see the answer to your query whether you were also under work assignment, because here we can see that you had your work assignment or work obligation and that it was in the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says here so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What we cannot see from this decision is the following. Whether you were, were you at all, appointed formally to this position of public prosecutor. Would you agree with me that it cannot be seen from this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes it cannot be seen in this document. I do know that I was appointed, I think it was in August. It was by the decree of the Serbian Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember having taken my oath in the district court in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me assist with you this. So you agree that, throughout this period, we have had a legally irregular situation with you. From the time of your appointment by the Executive Committee until the time you were appointed by the relevant state organ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: If one views it formally, yes. My appointment wasn't done according to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since we're discussing this Executive Committee, could you please tell me what power the local authorities had at the time, and I specifically mean Crisis Staffs. What were their powers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I think they had the crucial power. I think they had the main power vested in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will then agree with me that the result of such a role of this was your appointment for public prosecutor in the municipality of Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, this was their decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now resolve this issue of when was it that you were actually appointed so that the Trial Chamber is informed of that as well. Let us go back to document 872.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's from 65 ter list of the Prosecutor. It is tab number 84, I apologise; but 84 from the binder of Prosecutor's materials. I apologise, I failed to switch my mic on. I would like to ask the Court Officer whether you've managed to find this document, number 84? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, this is a report you've discussed with the Prosecutor a moment ago. This is your report on the crime situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You're stating in the second paragraph, referring to a decision of appointment by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic, and then we see the number and the date. And yes, you're right, the date is the 23rd of August, 1992. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we've resolved that issue. Yet I think you would agree with me, the appointment of -- by the Presidency is, again, a result of the situation; namely, the immediate threat of war, because at times like that, at times when the Assembly cannot convene, the Presidency was the organ that took over some of the Assembly's duties. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: No I don't think that is correct. I think the Assembly was the body appointing or electing the officials and then the Presidency would be actually just appointing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Fine. But it was in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before we move to the next document, this previous document, since the witness identified; namely, it's the document concerning his appointment, I would like to ask for it to be entered into evidence. It's 1D03-3322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This hasn't been previously exhibited? Yes, well, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D00274. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, since we have this report which is still on the screen, and before we remove it, could you help me just with one issue. I cannot see from this report whom it was addressed to? I don't see a date, the date of its drafting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: This is a separate document. There was another cover page. It would include my KTA number and the date of submitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that one cannot conclude from the document itself, neither to whom it was addressed, nor the date when it was drafted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that it was sent to the Municipal Assembly and most probably in early October, because it was for the two-months period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You mean the Municipal Assembly of Teslic? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Peric, let us move to a different topic. Let us briefly discuss constitutional and legal position of the public prosecutor as a member of the judicial system within Republika Srpska at the time, and maybe the best starting point for this exercise would be to take a look at how the constitution of the Republika Srpska defines your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit P181.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will find it under tab 24 in the binder that you have there. Just tell me when you have the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please. Which article?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: A bit of patience, please. I first must inform the Trial Chamber where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 10 of the B/C/S and page 21 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Specifically, we are interested in Article 133. I believe we have it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just scroll down in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This says literally that: "The office of the public prosecutor is an independent state agency prosecuting perpetrators of criminal offences and other punishable acts specified by law, and applies legal remedies in order to protect... legality." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the constitution briefly but effectively defines the role of the public prosecutor, tasking him or her with taking action against perpetrators of criminal and other offences.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I believe this is pretty unclear what is meant by taking action against or persecuting, as it says here in the English, because if we look at the Law on -- on Interior Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, please allow me to ask my questions. We are now interpreting the constitution and we are arguing that this is not precise enough?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then let us look at the decision on the basic organisation and the seats of public prosecutor's offices. Let us see document 1D03-3318.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours before -- before we come off this document, Judge Peric wanted to say something about the Law on Internal Affairs and was cut off. I think he ought to be allowed to answer it if it's on the point of the question he was being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We would have -- this issue would have arisen yesterday. Yes, the witness should be permitted and -- complete his answer, Mr. Cvijetic. Judge Peric --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave Your Honours, the Law on Internal Affairs is an exhibit on my list already, and I will discuss it with the witness but in a way and at the time I decide in my cross-examination. I will proceed in my sequence, and I will reach the Law on Internal Affairs yet. It is it contained in the binder which is in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may be so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Cvijetic, that if either in examination-in-chief or in cross-examination, a witness is asked a question and gives an answer, unless he is wondering off into irrelevancies, and that is something to which the Chamber would be alive, he should, as a matter of courtesy, be permitted to complete his answer. And to cut off a witness in mid-sentence is simply not proper. And I think that is the point that Ms. Korner was making. As I said, it is with which -- which arose yesterday, as recently as yesterday. I was about to ask the witness whether he remembers now the question that he was seeking to answer when the -- when this interruption occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wanted to explain the position of the public prosecutor's office and the bodies of the Ministry of Interior, that is, the police. It says here in the constitution that the public prosecutor's task is to prosecute the perpetrators of crimes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and start over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Judge Peric, the interpreters are having difficulty keeping up with you, so if you would be so kind as to slow down in your response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat. I wanted to explain the position of the public prosecutor and the bodies of the -- of Internal Affairs, that is the police. Under the Law on Criminal Procedure, the bodies of Internal Affairs were duty-bound to identify perpetrators of crimes and collect evidence and that is their crucial role; whereas, the prosecutor was duty-bound to launch a judicial proceedings based on that, and that is the distinction between the prosecutor and the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, both pieces of legislation that the witness mentioned, I was going to put to him anyway. But you have anticipated my questions. Very well. I asked for document 1D03-3318 to be displayed. That's under tab 26.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right. You can ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just bear with us. We have to see it on our screens first.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the translation of this document was pending. I'm not sure whether it is finished. Let us just check whether we have an English version available. If this is the English version, please show us the heading of the document. Let's scroll up. Is it this document? Yes. Well, we're interested in Article 2. We can see it on both versions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, the constitutional position of the public prosecutor's office is also defined by the decision on the main principles of the organisation, seat, and it's the territory of the public prosecutor's offices in the very way I said. But it is an autonomous state body which prosecute the perpetrators of crimes and other offences punishable by law -- by law, et cetera. Are you saying that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat his last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the interpreters did not get your last question. So if you would be good enough to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, it seems to me that this decision and Article 2 defines the position of the public prosecutor's office rather clearly. I fail to see what is unclear here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I suppose that this definition was taken over. This isn't any matter of organisational nature, so I don't see your point, but possibly this is a definition from the law. I am not denying that it is contained in this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It was taken over from the Law on Public Prosecutor's offices of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was applied based on the Constitutional Law for the Implementation of the Constitution of the Republika Srpska in which there was a provision, and you know that, to the effect that, in the RS until the adoption of relevant laws and other pieces of legislation, the laws and regulations of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are to be applied if they are in accordance with the constitution, et cetera. You know of this provision of the constitutional law by which the laws and regulations of the former Socialist Republic of BiH were taken over; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, then you have to agree with me when I say that the constitutional position of the public prosecutor in the RS is defined in the same way as it was in the Socialist Republic of BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC
utterances.text: I can agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, this line of question, has it a special -- a specific purpose in regard to this witness, or is this just a repetition of what we heard over and over again, in the -- in the recent past?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And before you attempt to answer Judge Delvoie's question, I would add a subquestion of my own: Is there no -- is -- there's no controversy, is there, as to the fact that the witness was in post in this legal public office performing the duties at the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, so far, we've only had the Constitutional Law About the Implementation of the Constitution, and we are referring to it often. But, now, for the first time, we meet regulations dealing with the work of the public prosecutor, which has not been the case so far, and we haven't had a public prosecutor yet either, so it's important for us define the position of the public prosecutor and the relations between him and the Internal Affairs; that is, the police. That is a relevant fact in this trial. Because the Defence does not fully agree with the definition of the relationship existing between the police and the public prosecutor's office as it was defined by the witness in his statement given to the Prosecution, which is part of the OTP set of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I suggest, Mr. Cvijetic, that it would be more helpful to the Trial Chamber if you were to proceed directly with your challenge to the witness as to how, as I understand what you have just said, he misapprehended or misappreciated the nature of his work in relation to other relevant agencies. Because otherwise it appears that we're heading down a -- either a -- into a purely academic exercise or the Chamber is being drawn into making a ruling on different interpretations of Bosnian law which we are certainly not competent to do. So if I understand your right, perhaps you should proceed directly to your challenge of the witness as to how he did perform his duties while he was in post.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to do all that, but I cannot before I provide references and show the laws and regulations, to set a foundation for the position of the Defence. I would first like to tender this decision into evidence because the witness clearly recognised the document establishing the organisation of the public prosecutor's offices. So let me repeat, 1D03-3318.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Wouldn't this be a matter for the law library rather than being tendered as an exhibit, as a specific exhibit, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a very brief decision, and it is -- it's a fact that only Article 2 is relevant on occasion of this testimony. I will also volunteer my personal opinion. I'm a pessimist with regard to the outlook of establishing this law library, so I would really prefer this to be tendered or admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As you say, it's a short decision so we'd mark it as an exhibit, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit number 1D00275. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the following document is an exhibit I wanted to show to the witness. He has already referred to it. It requires more time for me to deal with it, so with your leave, I propose that I continue with this document tomorrow. Because I might be able, just to finish one paragraph, and that is, I believe, not a good approach. We're nearing 7.00 anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Judge Peric, the Chamber is about to conclude its sitting for the day. We will resume, as I indicated to you earlier, at 9.00 our time tomorrow morning. And I am obliged to caution you, although having regard to your own profession you will readily appreciate this, but having been sworn as a witness you cannot discuss your testimony with anyone outside -- your testimony before the Tribunal with -- with other persons. So thank you, sir. We will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of May, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.55 p.m.,
